lessons.title: Lesson 1: Selecting Profitable Crops for Greenhouse Production in Africa
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 6, Lesson 1. In this lesson we focus on one of the most important business decisions you will make as a greenhouse farmer: choosing which crops to grow. A greenhouse is a significant investment, so every square meter must earn its keep. The wrong crop choice can tie up your capital, labour, and space for months with little return. The right choice can give you a steady income, premium prices, and repeat customers. We will look at high-value vegetables, market demand, crop cycles, and how to match crops to your local conditions and customer base. First, understand that greenhouse farming is not the same as open-field farming. You are paying for structure, irrigation, ventilation, and often labour. That means you should focus on crops that give high value per square meter, have strong demand, and can be grown reliably under protected conditions. In most African markets, the best greenhouse crops include tomatoes, sweet peppers, cucumbers, lettuce, spinach, kale, herbs such as basil and mint, and specialty crops like strawberries and cherry tomatoes. These crops respond well to controlled environments and can be sold at premium prices, especially when out of season. Tomatoes remain the most popular greenhouse crop across Africa. They are in constant demand, can be grown year-round in a greenhouse, and have a ready market in urban areas, hotels, restaurants, and supermarkets. However, tomatoes are also susceptible to diseases and pests, so you need good management. Choose varieties that are resistant to common problems such as bacterial wilt, fusarium wilt, and tomato yellow leaf curl virus. Determinate varieties are good for short cycles, while indeterminate varieties produce over a longer period and can be trained vertically to save space. Sweet peppers, especially coloured bell peppers, fetch high prices in cities. They require similar conditions to tomatoes but can be more delicate. Cucumbers are fast-growing and productive, but they need strong trellising and consistent watering. Leafy greens such as lettuce, spinach, and kale have short cycles, sometimes as short as 30 to 45 days, which means quick returns and the ability to plant many cycles per year. Herbs are lightweight, high-value, and popular with restaurants and health-conscious consumers. Strawberries are a specialty crop that can earn very high prices, but they need careful pollination and cool conditions. When selecting crops, start with your market. Who will buy your produce? Are there supermarkets, hotels, restaurants, schools, or open markets nearby? Talk to potential buyers before you plant. Ask what they need, what quantities, what quality standards, and what prices they pay. A common mistake is to grow what you like rather than what the market wants. For example, a farmer may love growing lettuce, but if the local market is flooded with lettuce, prices will be low. On the other hand, if you can supply fresh basil to a hotel that currently imports it, you can charge a premium. Next, consider your climate and greenhouse type. A naturally ventilated greenhouse works well in warm areas, but in very hot regions you may need shade nets and fogging systems. In cooler highland areas, you may need heating or thermal screens at night. Choose crops that match your climate. Tomatoes and peppers like warm days and cooler nights. Lettuce and spinach prefer cooler temperatures and may bolt in extreme heat. If your greenhouse gets very hot, focus on heat-tolerant crops such as okra, amaranth, or certain pepper varieties. If you are in a cooler area, you can grow a wider range of leafy greens and even strawberries. Crop cycles and succession planting are also key. Do not plant all your tomatoes at once. If you do, you will have a glut of tomatoes at harvest and then nothing for months. Instead, stagger planting every two to four weeks so you have continuous supply. This keeps your customers happy and your income steady. For leafy greens, you can harvest and replant quickly. For fruiting crops like tomatoes and peppers, plan for a longer season, often six to nine months. You can interplant quick crops like lettuce between rows of young tomatoes to use space efficiently before the tomatoes fill out. Another factor is labour. Some crops need more labour than others. Tomatoes need pruning, staking, and training. Cucumbers need trellising and frequent harvesting. Herbs need careful harvesting and packaging. Leafy greens need washing and bundling. Be realistic about how much labour you have or can hire. If labour is expensive or scarce, choose crops that need less hands-on work, such as certain leafy greens or peppers. If you have a family workforce, you can manage more intensive crops. Water and nutrients also matter. Greenhouse crops need consistent irrigation and fertigation. Drip irrigation is the standard. You need a reliable water source and a plan for mixing and applying nutrients. Some crops are heavy feeders, like tomatoes and cucumbers, while leafy greens need less. Test your water and soil or growing media regularly. In Africa, many greenhouse farmers use soil, but others use hydroponics or grow bags with coco peat or perlite. Each system has different crop suitability. Hydroponics works well for lettuce, herbs, and strawberries, while soil works well for tomatoes, peppers, and cucumbers. Pest and disease management is easier in a greenhouse, but not eliminated. You must scout regularly, use sticky traps, and practice good sanitation. Choose resistant varieties and rotate crops. Avoid planting the same family of crops in the same beds season after season. For example, do not follow tomatoes with peppers or eggplants because they share pests and diseases. Finally, think about your business model. Are you selling wholesale to a supermarket, retail at a farmers market, or direct to consumers through a box scheme? Each model has different crop requirements. Supermarkets want consistent size, colour, and packaging. Direct consumers may accept more variety and heirloom types. Restaurants want specific herbs and specialty vegetables. Your crop plan should match your sales channel. In summary, select crops based on market demand, price, climate suitability, crop cycle, labour, and your production system. Start with one or two main crops and a few secondary crops. Test small areas before scaling up. Keep records of yields, costs, and prices so you can make better decisions next season. Remember, a greenhouse is a business asset. Treat crop selection as a business decision, not a gardening hobby. In the next lesson, we will look at greenhouse climate control and how to manage temperature, humidity, and ventilation for healthy crops.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Managing Greenhouse Climate and Irrigation for Maximum Yields
lessons.body: Welcome to Lesson 2 of Module 6. Now that you have chosen your crops, the next step is to manage the greenhouse environment. Climate and irrigation are the two most powerful tools you have to influence plant growth, yield, and quality. In this lesson, we will cover temperature, humidity, ventilation, shading, and irrigation systems, with practical advice for African conditions. A greenhouse works by trapping heat and protecting plants from wind, rain, and pests. But without proper management, it can become too hot, too humid, or too dry. The goal is to create a stable environment that matches the needs of your crops. Most greenhouse vegetables grow best with daytime temperatures between 20 and 28 degrees Celsius and nighttime temperatures between 15 and 20 degrees Celsius. Leafy greens prefer cooler conditions, around 15 to 22 degrees Celsius. If temperatures rise above 30 degrees Celsius, many crops suffer heat stress, drop flowers, or become prone to disease. If temperatures drop below 10 degrees Celsius, growth slows or stops. In hot African regions, overheating is the biggest challenge. You need ventilation, shading, and sometimes evaporative cooling. Roll-up sides, ridge vents, and louvers allow hot air to escape. Place vents on opposite sides so air can flow through. Use insect screens on vents to keep pests out, but keep them clean to maintain airflow. Shade nets, either outside or inside the greenhouse, reduce solar radiation and lower temperatures by several degrees. A 30 to 50 percent shade net is common for tomatoes and peppers in hot areas. For lettuce, you may need 50 to 70 percent shade. Whitewash or reflective paint on the roof can also reduce heat. Evaporative cooling, using foggers or misters, can lower temperatures but also raises humidity. Use it carefully, especially in humid areas where it may not work well. In cooler highland areas, the challenge is keeping plants warm at night. Thermal screens or curtains can trap heat. You can also use small heaters, but they are expensive. A simpler approach is to seal gaps and use double-layer plastic. Choose crops that tolerate cooler nights, such as kale, spinach, and some lettuce varieties. Humidity is another critical factor. High humidity encourages fungal diseases such as powdery mildew, downy mildew, and botrytis. Low humidity causes plants to lose water and wilt. Most greenhouse vegetables prefer relative humidity between 60 and 80 percent. To reduce humidity, increase ventilation, avoid overwatering, and use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering. Water early in the day so leaves dry before evening. Remove weeds and dead plant material that can hold moisture. In very dry areas, you may need to increase humidity by wetting pathways or using misters, but be careful not to create disease conditions. Air circulation is essential. Even with vents, you need fans to move air within the greenhouse. Horizontal airflow fans keep air moving around plants, reducing condensation and strengthening stems. In large greenhouses, use a combination of roof vents, side vents, and circulation fans. Monitor temperature and humidity with simple instruments. A maximum-minimum thermometer tells you the high and low temperatures since you last checked. A hygrometer measures humidity. You can also buy inexpensive digital sensors that record data. Check them daily, preferably morning and afternoon. Keep a log so you can see patterns and make adjustments. Irrigation is the lifeline of your greenhouse. Plants need consistent moisture, but not too much or too little. Drip irrigation is the best method for greenhouse vegetables. It delivers water directly to the root zone, saves water, reduces weeds, and keeps foliage dry. You can use drip lines with emitters spaced according to your crop. For tomatoes and peppers, one or two drippers per plant is common. For lettuce, you can use drip tape with closer emitters. You also need a water source, a pump, a filter, and a tank for mixing nutrients. Fertigation, which is injecting soluble fertilisers into the irrigation water, is highly efficient. You can buy simple venturi injectors or dosing pumps. Start with a balanced fertiliser mix and adjust based on crop stage. Seedlings need less; fruiting plants need more potassium and calcium. Always test your water for pH and electrical conductivity. Most crops prefer pH between 5.8 and 6.5 in soil or growing media. Electrical conductivity, which measures nutrient concentration, should be around 1.5 to 2.5 for tomatoes and peppers, and lower for lettuce. Over-fertilising can burn roots and cause salt buildup. Under-fertilising causes pale leaves and poor yields. Monitor your plants for signs of nutrient deficiency. Yellow lower leaves may mean nitrogen deficiency. Purple leaves may mean phosphorus deficiency. Brown spots on leaves may mean calcium deficiency. Adjust your fertigation accordingly. Watering frequency depends on crop, stage, and weather. In hot weather, you may need to water several times a day. In cool weather, once a day or every other day may be enough. Use a timer or controller to automate irrigation. But do not rely blindly on timers. Check the soil or growing media by hand. It should be moist but not soggy. If you are using grow bags, lift them to feel the weight. Light bags need water. Mulching with plastic or organic material helps conserve moisture and suppress weeds. In Africa, water scarcity is a real concern. Harvest rainwater from greenhouse roofs into tanks. Use shade nets to reduce evaporation. Fix leaks immediately. Train your workers to check drip lines for clogging. Filters must be cleaned regularly. If you use borehole water, test for salinity and iron. High iron can clog emitters and harm plants. High salinity can stunt growth. You may need to leach the soil occasionally with extra water to flush salts. Climate and irrigation management go hand in hand. When it is hot and dry, plants transpire more, so they need more water. When it is cool and humid, they need less. Watch your plants. Wilting in the afternoon may be normal, but wilting in the morning means you need to water. Leaf curling, yellowing, or stunted growth are signs of stress. Keep a daily routine. In the morning, open vents and check irrigation. At midday, check temperature and shade. In the afternoon, close vents early enough to trap some warmth for the night. In the evening, inspect for pests and diseases. Record everything. Your records will help you fine-tune your system. Consider investing in simple automation. A thermostat can open vents automatically. A timer can control irrigation. A humidity sensor can turn on fans. These tools save labour and prevent mistakes. But they need maintenance and calibration. Start simple and add technology as your profits grow. Finally, remember that climate management is not just about equipment. It is about observation and response. Walk through your greenhouse every day. Look at the leaves, the soil, the sky. Feel the air. Smell the soil. Your senses are powerful tools. Combine them with instruments and records. In the next lesson, we will cover pest and disease management in the greenhouse, focusing on integrated pest management and safe pesticide use.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Integrated Pest and Disease Management in Greenhouse Vegetables
lessons.body: Welcome to Lesson 3 of Module 6. Pests and diseases can destroy your greenhouse investment quickly if you are not prepared. In this lesson, we will cover integrated pest management, or IPM, which combines prevention, monitoring, biological control, and safe chemical use. The goal is to keep pest and disease pressure low while protecting your workers, customers, and the environment. The first principle of IPM is prevention. A clean greenhouse is a healthy greenhouse. Start with sanitation. Remove weeds, crop residues, and old plant material from inside and around the greenhouse. These can harbour pests and diseases. Clean tools, boots, and hands before entering. Use a footbath with disinfectant at the entrance. If you visit other farms, change clothes and shoes before entering your greenhouse. Buy certified disease-free seeds and seedlings. If you raise your own seedlings, use clean trays and sterile growing media. Do not reuse media that had diseased plants. Quarantine new plants for a few days before introducing them to the main greenhouse. Use insect screens on all vents and doors. Repair tears in plastic or screens immediately. Pests such as whiteflies, aphids, and thrips are small enough to pass through standard mesh, so use fine mesh, ideally 50 to 100 mesh. Keep the area around the greenhouse mowed and free of weeds. Some weeds host pests and viruses. Rotate crops. Do not plant the same crop family in the same beds season after season. For example, after tomatoes, plant lettuce or beans instead of peppers or eggplants. This breaks pest and disease cycles. Consider soil solarisation if you have soil-borne problems. This involves covering moist soil with clear plastic for several weeks during hot weather. The heat kills many pathogens and weed seeds. Use resistant varieties whenever possible. Seed companies offer tomatoes resistant to fusarium wilt, verticillium wilt, and nematodes. Peppers resistant to bacterial spot are also available. Resistance is not immunity, but it reduces losses. The second principle is monitoring. You cannot manage what you do not measure. Scout your greenhouse at least twice a week. Walk in a zigzag pattern and inspect plants randomly. Look at the undersides of leaves, growing tips, flowers, and stems. Use a hand lens to see small pests. Yellow sticky traps are excellent for monitoring whiteflies, aphids, thrips, and leafminers. Place them just above the plant canopy, about one trap per 100 square meters. Check traps weekly and replace them when covered. Blue sticky traps attract thrips. Pheromone traps can monitor moths. Keep a record of pest numbers and locations. This helps you decide when to act. The third principle is biological control. This means using natural enemies to control pests. Many beneficial insects are available in Africa, though supply can be limited. You can also conserve natural enemies already present. Ladybirds eat aphids. Lacewing larvae eat aphids, thrips, and whitefly eggs. Parasitic wasps lay eggs inside whitefly and aphid larvae. Predatory mites eat spider mites. To encourage these beneficials, avoid broad-spectrum pesticides that kill them. Plant flowers such as marigolds, sunflowers, and basil around the greenhouse to provide nectar and pollen for adult beneficials. You can also buy and release beneficials. For example, Encarsia formosa is a wasp that controls whitefly. Phytoseiulus persimilis is a mite that controls spider mites. Bacillus thuringiensis, or Bt, is a bacterium that kills caterpillar larvae. It is safe for humans and beneficials. Trichoderma is a fungus that protects roots from soil-borne diseases. These biological products are increasingly available in African agro-dealer shops and online. The fourth principle is mechanical and physical control. Handpick large pests such as caterpillars and snails. Use barriers such as copper tape for slugs. Use water sprays to knock aphids off plants. Use reflective mulches to repel thrips and aphids. Use row covers for young seedlings, but remove them when flowering begins so pollinators can enter. In greenhouses, you may need to pollinate manually. Tomatoes need vibration to release pollen. You can use an electric toothbrush or a vibrating wand to buzz the flowers. Do this every two days in the morning. Bumblebees are excellent pollinators but may not be available everywhere. If you use bees, do not use pesticides during flowering. The fifth principle is chemical control, used as a last resort. When you must use pesticides, choose the least toxic option that is effective. Always read the label. Use the correct dose. Do not mix more than needed. Wear protective clothing: gloves, mask, goggles, long sleeves, and boots. Spray in the early morning or late evening when beneficials are less active and temperatures are cooler. Do not spray when it is windy or when rain is expected. Observe the pre-harvest interval, which is the time between spraying and harvest. Never harvest before the interval has passed. Rotate chemical groups to prevent resistance. Do not use the same active ingredient repeatedly. Common pests in African greenhouses include whiteflies, aphids, thrips, spider mites, leafminers, and caterpillars. Whiteflies suck sap and transmit viruses. Control them with yellow sticky traps, Encarsia wasps, neem oil, or insecticidal soap. Aphids also suck sap and transmit viruses. Control with ladybirds, lacewings, neem oil, or soap sprays. Thrips cause silvery streaks on leaves and damage flowers. Control with blue sticky traps, predatory mites, or spinosad. Spider mites cause yellow stippling and fine webbing. Control with predatory mites, neem oil, or sulfur sprays. Leafminers make winding tunnels in leaves. Control with yellow sticky traps, parasitic wasps, or removing affected leaves. Caterpillars chew holes in leaves and fruits. Control with Bt, handpicking, or neem oil. Common diseases include powdery mildew, downy mildew, botrytis, fusarium wilt, bacterial wilt, and viruses. Powdery mildew appears as white powder on leaves. It thrives in humid conditions with poor airflow. Control by improving ventilation, removing affected leaves, and using sulfur or potassium bicarbonate sprays. Downy mildew causes yellow patches on the upper leaf surface and fuzzy growth underneath. It spreads in cool, wet conditions. Control by reducing humidity, improving airflow, and using copper-based sprays. Botrytis causes grey mould on stems, leaves, and fruits, especially in cool, humid conditions. Remove affected parts and improve ventilation. Fusarium and bacterial wilt cause wilting and yellowing. There is no cure. Remove and destroy affected plants. Solarise soil or use resistant varieties. Viruses cause mosaic patterns, curling, and stunting. They are spread by pests. Control the pests and remove infected plants immediately. Do not compost diseased plants. Burn or bury them deep. Keep a spray diary. Record the date, pest or disease, product used, dose, and weather. This helps you evaluate what works and what does not. It also helps with traceability if you sell to supermarkets. Train your workers on safe pesticide handling. Store pesticides in a locked cabinet away from food and feed. Never store pesticides in drink bottles. Dispose of empty containers safely. Do not burn them or throw them in rivers. In summary, IPM is a system, not a single action. It combines sanitation, resistant varieties, monitoring, biological control, and careful chemical use. It takes more thought than spraying every week, but it produces healthier crops, lower costs, and safer food. In the next lesson, we will cover harvesting, post-harvest handling, and marketing your greenhouse produce.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Harvesting, Post-Harvest Handling, and Marketing Greenhouse Vegetables
lessons.body: Welcome to Lesson 4 of Module 6. You have grown your crops, managed the climate, and controlled pests. Now comes the moment of truth: harvesting and selling. How you harvest, handle, and market your produce determines your income. Poor post-harvest handling can destroy the value of months of work. In this lesson, we will cover harvest timing, tools, cooling, grading, packaging, and marketing strategies for African greenhouse farmers. Harvest timing is critical. Vegetables are living products. They continue to respire, lose water, and change after harvest. The goal is to harvest at the right maturity for the market. For tomatoes, harvest at the breaker stage, when the fruit is starting to turn from green to pink, if you are shipping long distances. For local sales, harvest when fully red but still firm. For peppers, harvest when they reach full colour and size. For cucumbers, harvest when they are young and tender, before seeds harden. For lettuce, harvest in the cool of the morning when leaves are crisp. For herbs, harvest before flowering for best flavour. Do not harvest wet crops. Wet leaves and fruits are more prone to disease. Wait until dew has dried. Use clean, sharp tools. Knives, secateurs, and harvest shears should be disinfected regularly. Dull tools bruise produce and create entry points for disease. Wear clean gloves. Do not throw produce into buckets. Place it gently. Use shallow crates or baskets to avoid crushing. Never pile produce too high. For tomatoes, harvest into small crates and do not stack more than three or four layers. For leafy greens, harvest into bunches and place them upright in clean crates. For herbs, cut stems and place them in water or a cool box immediately. After harvest, move produce out of the sun as quickly as possible. Heat is the enemy. Even a few minutes in direct sun can reduce shelf life. If you have a cold room, use it. If not, create a shaded, ventilated area. You can use evaporative cooling by placing wet sacks over crates in a breezy place. This can lower temperatures by several degrees. Do not wash produce unless necessary. Washing can spread disease and shorten shelf life. If you must wash, use clean water with a small amount of food-grade sanitizer. Dry gently with clean cloths or air dry. For leafy greens, washing is often expected by supermarkets, so follow their guidelines. Grading is sorting produce by size, colour, and quality. Grading adds value and makes your product more attractive. Buyers pay more for consistent quality. Grade tomatoes into uniform sizes and colours. Remove any with cracks, spots, or soft spots. Grade peppers by colour and size. Grade lettuce by head size and leaf quality. Grade herbs by stem length and leaf condition. Use a simple grading table under shade. Train your workers to grade consistently. Packaging protects produce and makes it easy to handle. Use clean, food-grade crates, boxes, or bags. Do not use fertiliser bags or chemical containers. For supermarkets, you may need branded punnets or bags. For local markets, simple crates are fine. Label your packages with your farm name, product, and date. This builds trust and traceability. For tomatoes, use vented crates so air can circulate. For leafy greens, use crates with liners to prevent wilting. For herbs, use bunches tied with clean string or bands. Do not overpack. Leave space for air. Stack crates carefully to avoid crushing. Transport is a major challenge in Africa. Poor roads, heat, and delays can ruin produce. Use covered vehicles or tarpaulins to protect from sun and rain. Load carefully. Do not overload. Drive smoothly. If possible, transport in the early morning or evening when it is cooler. For long distances, consider refrigerated trucks, but they are expensive. Many farmers use insulated boxes with ice packs for high-value crops like herbs and strawberries. Marketing is about knowing your customer and delivering value. There are several channels. Direct sales at farmers markets give you the best prices but require time and transport. Restaurants and hotels pay well but demand consistent quality and delivery. Supermarkets offer volume but often pay late and require strict standards. Schools, hospitals, and catering companies are reliable buyers. Neighbours and local shops are convenient but may pay less. Choose channels that match your production capacity and location. Before you plant, talk to buyers. Ask what they want, when they want it, and what price they pay. Get agreements in writing if possible. Do not rely on one buyer. Diversify. If one buyer stops, you still have income. Build relationships. Deliver on time. Be honest about quality. If you have a problem, communicate early. Consider value addition. You can wash and pack lettuce into ready-to-eat bags. You can dry herbs. You can make tomato sauce or chutney. You can make pickles from cucumbers. Value addition increases shelf life and profit, but it requires investment in equipment and food safety. Start small and test the market. Pricing is tricky. Calculate your cost of production per kilogram or per head. Include seeds, fertiliser, water, labour, packaging, transport, and a portion of your greenhouse investment. Add a profit margin. Check market prices. Do not undercut yourself. If you sell too cheap, you cannot reinvest. If you sell too high, you may not sell. Adjust based on feedback. Keep records of every sale. Track which crops are most profitable. Track which buyers pay best. Use this information to plan next season. Consider branding. A simple logo and farm name can make your produce stand out. Use social media to tell your story. Show photos of your greenhouse, your harvest, and your happy customers. Many urban consumers want to know where their food comes from. You can sell directly through WhatsApp groups, Facebook Marketplace, or local delivery apps. Offer a weekly box of mixed vegetables. This builds a loyal customer base. Food safety is essential. Buyers are increasingly demanding safe food. Use clean water. Use approved pesticides. Follow pre-harvest intervals. Keep your greenhouse and packing area clean. Train workers in hygiene. Wash hands. Wear clean clothes. Do not work when sick. Keep pests and animals out of the packing area. If you sell to supermarkets, you may need a food safety certification. Start with good practices and work towards certification. Finally, learn from every harvest. What went well? What went wrong? What will you do differently? Talk to other farmers. Join a cooperative or farmer group. Share transport, buy inputs in bulk, and negotiate better prices together. In the next lesson, we will cover record keeping, financial management, and scaling your greenhouse business.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Record Keeping, Financial Management, and Scaling Your Greenhouse Business
lessons.body: Welcome to Lesson 5 of Module 6. You have learned how to select crops, manage climate, control pests, and market your produce. Now we focus on the business side: record keeping, financial management, and scaling. Many greenhouse farmers fail not because they cannot grow crops, but because they do not manage money well. In this lesson, we will cover simple records, cost calculation, cash flow, profit, and strategies for growth. Record keeping is the foundation of good management. You cannot make good decisions without accurate information. Start with a simple notebook or a spreadsheet on a phone or computer. Record every expense and every sale. Record daily activities such as planting, fertilising, spraying, and harvesting. Record weather, pest outbreaks, and crop performance. Use a separate page for each crop or greenhouse section. At the end of each week, review your records. At the end of each month, calculate your income and expenses. At the end of each season, calculate your profit. What records do you need? First, input records. List all seeds, seedlings, fertilisers, pesticides, growing media, and packaging. Record the date, quantity, and cost. Second, labour records. Record who worked, for how many hours, and what they did. If you pay daily or monthly, record the amount. Include your own labour as a cost, even if you do not pay yourself. Third, production records. Record planting dates, crop varieties, number of plants, and expected harvest dates. Record actual harvest dates, quantities, and quality. Fourth, sales records. Record the date, buyer, product, quantity, price, and total. Record any discounts or losses. Fifth, financial records. Record all cash in and cash out. Keep receipts and invoices. Separate business money from personal money. Open a bank account or mobile money account for the business. Do not mix. Cost calculation is essential for pricing and profit. There are two types of costs: fixed and variable. Fixed costs do not change with production. They include greenhouse construction, irrigation system, tools, and land rent. Variable costs change with production. They include seeds, fertiliser, pesticides, labour, water, and packaging. To calculate the cost per unit, add all fixed and variable costs for a season and divide by the number of units harvested. For example, if you spent 5,000 on a tomato crop and harvested 2,000 kilograms, your cost per kilogram is 2.50. If you sell at 4.00 per kilogram, your profit is 1.50 per kilogram. But do not forget to include your own labour and a portion of the greenhouse cost. Many farmers forget these and think they are profitable when they are not. Cash flow is different from profit. You can be profitable on paper but run out of cash. This happens when you spend money before you earn it. Greenhouse farming has high upfront costs. You buy seeds, fertiliser, and labour before harvest. You need cash reserves or credit to bridge the gap. Plan your cash flow. Estimate when you will spend and when you will earn. Keep a buffer for emergencies. If you have a harvest delay or a price drop, you need reserves. Avoid borrowing too much. If you must borrow, borrow for productive assets, not for daily expenses. Compare interest rates. Use mobile money loans or cooperative loans if they are cheaper than banks. Repay on time to build credit. Profit is income minus all costs. Reinvest part of your profit into the business. Save part for emergencies. Pay yourself a salary. Many farmers take money from the business without recording it. This leads to confusion and loss. Decide on a monthly salary and stick to it. Scaling means growing your business. There are several ways to scale. You can increase the number of greenhouses. You can increase the yield per square meter. You can add value to your products. You can add new markets. You can add new crops. But do not scale too fast. Grow step by step. First, master one greenhouse. Get consistent yields and profits. Then add a second greenhouse. Use profits from the first to fund the second. Avoid heavy debt. Consider leasing land or sharing facilities with other farmers. Join a cooperative to buy inputs in bulk and sell together. Cooperatives can also help with transport and storage. Use technology to improve efficiency. Drip irrigation, timers, and sensors save water and labour. A smartphone can help you track records, check market prices, and communicate with buyers. Solar panels can power pumps and fans in areas with unreliable electricity. Train your workers. A skilled worker is more productive. Teach them about crop management, pest control, and post-harvest handling. Pay fair wages. Happy workers are less likely to steal or leave. Build a team. Delegate tasks. Do not try to do everything yourself. As you grow, you will need a farm manager, a salesperson, and a record keeper. Hire slowly and train well. Diversify your markets. Do not rely on one buyer. Sell to supermarkets, restaurants, schools, and directly to consumers. If one market fails, others will support you. Diversify your crops. Grow a mix of quick crops like lettuce and long-term crops like tomatoes. This smooths income and spreads risk. Consider value addition. Washing, cutting, and packaging vegetables can increase prices. Drying herbs, making sauces, or pickling cucumbers can extend shelf life and create new products. But value addition requires food safety and packaging skills. Start small and test. Plan for risks. Drought, floods, pests, disease, price drops, and theft can affect your business. Insurance may be available for crops or greenhouses. Ask about it. Keep some savings. Have a backup

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Lesson 6: Practical Reference for Greenhouse Vegetable Farming in Africa

This practical reference lesson consolidates the key operational data, safety protocols, and decision-support tools that greenhouse vegetable farmers across Africa need to run a profitable, compliant, and resilient operation. It is designed as a standalone quick-access guide that complements Lessons 1â5. All figures are drawn from official sources and are intended for business planning, budgeting, and day-to-day management. Whether you are running a 200 mÂ² tunnel in Kenya or a 5,000 mÂ² multi-span greenhouse in South Africa, the reference tables, safety warnings, and checklists below will help you make faster, better decisions.

Table 1: Yield and Water-Use Benchmarks for Major Greenhouse Vegetables in Africa

The table below provides realistic yield ranges and water-use efficiency benchmarks for the most commonly grown greenhouse vegetables in sub-Saharan Africa. Use these figures to set production targets and to evaluate whether your operation is performing at, above, or below regional norms. Data are drawn from FAO horticultural production reports and validated by regional extension trials in Kenya, Ethiopia, and South Africa.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â PESTICIDE HANDLING AND FOOD SAFETY

Greenhouse environments concentrate pesticide residues and vapours. All operators must follow these mandatory precautions:

  • Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): Always wear gloves, coveralls, boots, and a respirator approved for chemical use when mixing or applying pesticides. Never enter a treated greenhouse for at least the label-specified re-entry interval (REI), typically 12â24 hours.
  • Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): Strictly observe the PHI on every product label. Harvesting before the PHI expires leaves illegal residues that can cause illness and lead to rejection at export markets. This is a legal requirement under WHO/FAO Codex Alimentarius standards.
  • Storage: Store all agrochemicals in a locked, ventilated, labelled cabinet away from food, feed, and water sources. Never decant pesticides into beverage containers.
  • Disposal: Triple-rinse empty containers and puncture them. Never reuse pesticide containers for water or food. Dispose of according to national regulations.
  • Health: If you experience dizziness, nausea, blurred vision, or skin irritation after handling chemicals, stop work immediately, move to fresh air, and seek medical attention. Report all incidents.

Source: World Health Organization (WHO) Recommended Classification of Pesticides by Hazard and Guidelines to Classification (2019); FAO/WHO International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management (2014).

Quick Reference Checklist: Daily and Weekly Greenhouse Operations

Use this checklist to maintain consistency and catch problems before they become costly. Print it and keep it in your greenhouse record book.

  1. Daily â Climate check: Record maximum and minimum temperatures, relative humidity, and ventilation status. Open vents early on sunny days to prevent heat stress and fungal disease.
  2. Daily â Irrigation and fertigation: Check soil moisture or substrate weight. Verify EC and pH of the nutrient solution. Adjust irrigation duration based on weather and crop stage.
  3. Daily â Crop scouting: Walk the crop and inspect leaves (upper and lower surfaces), stems, and fruit for pests, disease symptoms, and nutrient deficiencies. Record findings and take action within 24 hours.
  4. Weekly â Pest and disease monitoring: Check sticky traps and pheromone traps. Count and record pest numbers. Release biocontrol agents if thresholds are reached. Remove and destroy severely infested plants.
  5. Weekly â Nutrition and soil/substrate testing: Send samples for laboratory analysis every 2â4 weeks, or use on-site meters. Adjust fertiliser recipe based on crop stage and analysis results.
  6. Weekly â Record keeping: Update your records for inputs used, labour hours, yields, and sales. Calculate your gross margin weekly to track profitability.
  7. Weekly â Maintenance: Inspect the greenhouse structure, irrigation lines, drippers, and vents for leaks, blockages, or damage. Repair immediately to avoid crop loss.
  8. Monthly â Financial review: Reconcile income and expenditure. Compare actual performance against your budget. Adjust pricing, marketing, or production plans as needed.

quiz.q: Which environmental factor most directly controls the rate of transpiration in a greenhouse tomato crop?
quiz.explanation: Vapor pressure deficit combines temperature and humidity and drives the water vapor gradient between leaf and air, so it most directly controls transpiration rate.

quiz.q: In greenhouse vegetable production, what is the primary purpose of injecting carbon dioxide?
options: A) To sterilize the root zone
B) To increase photosynthesis and yield
quiz.explanation: Carbon dioxide enrichment raises the substrate for photosynthesis, often increasing growth and marketable yield when light and other factors are adequate.

quiz.q: Which practice best prevents blossom end rot in greenhouse peppers and tomatoes?
options: C) Maintaining consistent calcium uptake and irrigation
quiz.explanation: Blossom end rot is linked to calcium deficiency in the fruit caused by irregular water supply, so consistent irrigation and calcium uptake are key.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of using bumblebees instead of manual vibration for pollinating greenhouse tomatoes?
options: A) They eliminate the need for pruning
D) They improve fruit set and reduce labor
quiz.explanation: Bumblebees pollinate flowers efficiently, improving fruit set and size while reducing the labor required for manual pollination.

quiz.q: Which integrated pest management step should be taken first when a new pest is detected in a greenhouse vegetable crop?
options: A) Correctly identify the pest and monitor its population
B) Apply a broad spectrum pesticide immediately
C) Increase irrigation to wash off pests
D) Remove all plants from the greenhouse
quiz.explanation: Accurate identification and monitoring are the foundation of IPM because they determine whether and which control action is justified.

quiz.q: Why is root zone heating often beneficial for greenhouse cucumbers in cool climates?
options: A) It increases leaf transpiration to wilting
B) It supports root activity and nutrient uptake
C) It eliminates the need for carbon dioxide
D) It prevents all fungal diseases
quiz.explanation: Warming the root zone keeps roots active in cool conditions, improving water and nutrient uptake and supporting steady crop growth.

quiz.q: What does electrical conductivity of the nutrient solution primarily indicate in hydroponic greenhouse vegetables?
options: C) The total concentration of dissolved salts
D) The calcium to magnesium ratio only
quiz.explanation: Electrical conductivity measures the ability of the solution to conduct electricity, which reflects the total dissolved salt concentration available to the crop.

quiz.q: Which strategy best reduces the risk of powdery mildew in a greenhouse cucumber crop?
options: D) Managing humidity and increasing air movement
quiz.explanation: Powdery mildew thrives in humid, stagnant air, so controlling humidity and improving air movement reduce leaf wetness and disease pressure.

quiz.q: Which factor is most important when selecting a profitable greenhouse crop in Africa?
options: A) High market demand and short growing cycle
B) Large seed size and deep roots
C) Low light requirement and long dormancy
D) High water consumption and slow growth
quiz.explanation: Crops with strong local demand and quick turnover generate faster returns and reduce risk for African greenhouse farmers.

quiz.q: Which crop is commonly grown in African greenhouses for high-value export and local markets?
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes are a leading greenhouse crop in Africa due to high demand, good yields, and strong market prices.

quiz.q: Why should a farmer consider market proximity when choosing a greenhouse crop?
options: A) It reduces the need for irrigation
C) It lowers transport costs and spoilage
D) It eliminates the need for record keeping
quiz.explanation: Selling near the farm reduces transport costs and post-harvest losses, improving profit margins.

quiz.q: Which greenhouse climate factor most directly affects photosynthesis and yield?
quiz.explanation: Light drives photosynthesis, so managing light intensity and day length is critical for maximum yields.

quiz.q: What is the ideal purpose of ventilation in a greenhouse?
options: A) To increase humidity to 100 percent
B) To control temperature and humidity
quiz.explanation: Ventilation removes excess heat and moisture, preventing disease and heat stress.

quiz.q: Which irrigation method is most efficient for greenhouse vegetables?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to roots, saving water and reducing foliar disease.

quiz.q: What does EC measure in greenhouse irrigation water?
options: A) Electrical conductivity and nutrient concentration
quiz.explanation: EC indicates dissolved salts and nutrient strength, helping farmers avoid over or under fertilization.

quiz.q: Which practice helps prevent heat stress in a greenhouse during hot African afternoons?
options: C) Increasing plant spacing to zero
quiz.explanation: Shade netting reduces incoming radiation and lowers internal temperature during peak heat.

quiz.q: What is the first step of integrated pest management in greenhouses?
options: B) Identify pests and monitor populations
quiz.explanation: IPM starts with correct identification and monitoring before choosing control actions.

quiz.q: Which biological control agent is commonly used against whiteflies in greenhouses?
quiz.explanation: Encarsia formosa is a parasitic wasp that controls whitefly populations naturally.

quiz.q: Why is crop rotation difficult but important in greenhouse vegetable production?
options: B) It breaks pest and disease cycles
C) It eliminates the need for fertilizer
quiz.explanation: Rotating crops disrupts soilborne pests and diseases that build up in continuous cropping systems.

quiz.q: Which disease is favored by high humidity and poor air circulation in greenhouses?
quiz.explanation: Powdery mildew thrives in humid, stagnant air, so ventilation and spacing are key controls.

quiz.q: What is the best time to harvest most greenhouse vegetables for peak quality?
options: A) During the hottest part of the day
B) In the early morning or late evening
D) After several days of storage
quiz.explanation: Cooler times reduce field heat and preserve freshness, extending shelf life.

quiz.q: Which post-harvest practice reduces spoilage of greenhouse vegetables?
options: A) Leaving produce in direct sun
quiz.explanation: Pre-cooling removes field heat and slows deterioration, maintaining quality.

quiz.q: Why is grading important before marketing greenhouse vegetables?
options: B) It ensures uniform quality and better prices
C) It reduces the need for packaging
quiz.explanation: Grading creates uniform lots that meet buyer standards and attract higher prices.

quiz.q: Which marketing channel often gives greenhouse farmers the best price in Africa?
options: A) Selling at farm gate to neighbors
B) Direct supply to supermarkets and hotels
quiz.explanation: Supermarkets and hotels pay premium prices for consistent, high-quality greenhouse produce.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of keeping farm records?
options: B) To track costs, yields, and profits
quiz.explanation: Records reveal financial performance and guide better management decisions.

quiz.q: Which record is most useful for calculating the profitability of a greenhouse crop?
options: B) Input costs and sales revenue
quiz.explanation: Comparing input costs with sales revenue shows whether the crop is profitable.

quiz.q: What does break-even analysis tell a greenhouse farmer?
options: A) The exact color of the crop
B) The sales needed to cover costs
D) The number of leaves per plant
quiz.explanation: Break-even analysis identifies the minimum sales volume or price needed to avoid losses.

quiz.q: Which strategy helps scale a greenhouse business sustainably?
options: B) Reinvesting profits and improving efficiency
D) Growing every crop at once
quiz.explanation: Reinvestment and efficiency gains support controlled, sustainable expansion.

quiz.q: What is a practical reference for determining greenhouse irrigation frequency?
options: A) Plant appearance and soil moisture sensors
quiz.explanation: Observing plants and using moisture sensors ensures irrigation matches crop needs.

quiz.q: Which financial practice helps a greenhouse farmer prepare for unexpected losses?
quiz.explanation: A contingency fund provides a buffer against pests, weather, or market shocks.
